clinicalVerdict: Correct throughout, and the column wording is unusually careful. Row q2_r1 is right: curiosity is not a treatment, payment or health-care-operations purpose. Row q2_r2 is right: an identifiable image on a personal device without consent is a completed impermissible creation of a record. Row q2_r3 is right AND the column wording is what makes it right - I tested this specifically, because a workers' compensation request is a genuine trap. Verified at 45 CFR 164.512(l): a covered entity 'may disclose protected health information as authorized by and to the extent necessary to comply with laws relating to workers' compensation', without individual authorisation. Had the column read 'only after authorization', the key would have been wrong; it reads 'after authorization OR legal basis is verified through the proper process', which correctly accommodates the workers' compensation pathway while still denying the unit nurse the right to release. Row q2_r4 is right: spousal status does not itself authorise disclosure, and under 45 CFR 164.510(b)(2), which I read in full earlier in this review, disclosure to a family member for a present and capacitated patient requires the individual's agreement, an unobjected opportunity to object, or a reasonable professional inference - and here the caller's identity is not even verified. Row q2_r5 is right: incidental disclosures are permitted only where reasonable safeguards and minimum necessary are applied, and naming a patient and HIV status within visitor earshot fails that standard. I also checked the column set for the false-exclusivity defect found in several other matrices in this population and it is ABSENT here: the three columns describe genuinely disjoint pathways - internal access, external request, verbal communication - so single_per_row is appropriate.

clinicalVerdict: Four of the five keyed actions are clearly correct and the single distractor is correct and well grounded. Keyed q4_a, q4_b, q4_c and q4_e each contain the exposure and route the matter appropriately, and q4_c is right for the reason verified on the sibling row - a workers' compensation request may have a legal basis, but verifying it belongs to health information management rather than the unit nurse. Distractor q4_f is decisively wrong on the case's own stated policy, which says incident reports 'must not be referenced in the medical record'. THE DEFECT IS IN KEYED OPTION q4_d, which directs an irreversible act on evidence without any supplied procedure authorising it. The option has the nurse delete the identifiable photograph immediately, including recently deleted storage, on a personal device. Nothing in HIPAA mandates this, and the case's own policy does not specify it; the policy says only to mitigate exposure. The tension is real rather than academic. Under 45 CFR 164.402, read directly, whether this event is a reportable breach is settled by a four-factor risk assessment that considers the nature and extent of the protected health information involved including the types of identifiers, whether the information was actually acquired or viewed, the unauthorised recipient, and the extent to which the risk has been mitigated. Witnessed deletion serves the fourth factor, but destroying the image before the Privacy Officer's determination removes the primary evidence for the first and third. The item therefore teaches one specific irreversible institutional procedure as though it were the universally correct nursing action, in a case that never supplies that procedure, and it does so for the one action among the five that cannot be undone if wrong.
contentDefects: PRIMARY: keyed option q4_d directs immediate permanent deletion including recently deleted storage, an irreversible destruction of potential breach evidence, with no institutional procedure supplied in the case to authorise it and no basis in HIPAA, which nowhere mandates deletion.
CONTRIBUTING: the same unsupported procedure is narrated as correct practice in the stage_2 exhibit, so the defect exists on two surfaces and must be repaired on both together.

OBSERVATION: the item's own byChoice for q4_d concedes the difficulty - 'Immediate deletion limits exposure, but reporting is still needed because cloud syncing or other retention must be investigated' - which acknowledges that the image's fate is not fully within the nurse's control and that investigation continues after the deletion.

repairConstraints: Choose one of two routes and apply it to BOTH the q4_d option and the stage_2 exhibit sentence, in EN and ZH.

Route A, confined and recommended: revise q4_d so the nurse contains the exposure and escalates without asserting irreversible destruction - stop any further sharing, secure the image and the device pending Privacy Officer or security direction, and report immediately - leaving the disposition of the image to the Privacy Officer. This preserves the teaching point (contain and report) and removes the unsupported procedure.

Route B, shared surface: author a specific institutional photo-incident procedure into the baseline policy exhibit, including how evidence is preserved for the breach determination, so that the keyed deletion is grounded in the case's own policy. This edits a global surface visible to all six parts and requires re-review of the four baseline-anchored siblings.
Under either route, do not present HIPAA as universally mandating immediate permanent deletion.

criticalNote: RESOLUTION OF PRODUCER REVIEW_HOLD. Codex held this row over whether a permanent-deletion response lacking a specified evidence-preserving incident procedure can be keyed. I resolve it as a content repair rather than leaving it open. Codex's two routes are the right two, and its caution not to present HIPAA as universally mandating immediate permanent deletion is correct and I adopt it as a binding constraint.
